An integration is how you point HotLoop at a kind of device you know the
address of, answer a few questions, see what is actually on it, and keep the
points you want. It makes the device and its tags. Entities follow from the tags
the way they do for every tag, so the new points are on the entity API, in
automations and on dashboards a minute later.

There are three ways a device gets into HotLoop, and they are meant to sit side
by side:

| <span class="sr-only">Details</span> | Who starts it | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| [MQTT discovery](/iot/mqtt-discovery/) | The device, by announcing itself on a broker | A publisher that speaks one of the formats |
| [Network discovery](/iot/network-discovery/) | The network, by being listened to | Nothing from the device; it tells you what it heard and how HotLoop could talk to it |
| **Integrations** (this page) | You, with an address | A device that answers its own protocol |

An integration never writes to the device, and nothing it makes is armed. A
point that was found is a point nobody has yet decided may be commanded, so
every tag a setup creates is read-only until someone arms it, one at a time, in
the tag editor, the same as a tag from any other source.

## What is here

| Integration | Protocol | Verified against |
|---|---|---|
| OPC UA server (`opcua`) | [OPC UA](/iot/protocols/#opc-ua) | Microsoft's opc-plc 2.12.48 |
| SNMP device (`snmp`) | [SNMP](/iot/protocols/#snmp) | net-snmp's `snmpd` 5.9.4, v1, v2c and v3 |
| BACnet/IP device (`bacnet`) | [BACnet/IP](/iot/protocols/#bacnetip) | bacpypes3 0.0.110, an independent BACnet stack |

More are added on this framework as they can be proven against a real server.

## SNMP

For a switch, a UPS, a PDU, a power meter, or anything running an SNMP agent. The
questions follow the version: v2c asks for a community, v3 asks for a user and
only the passphrases its security level needs. There is no default community.

The probe walks the system group, the interface tables, host resources, the
load table and net-snmp's extend outputs, the objects HotLoop can name, and
shows each with what the agent said it holds right now. It **suggests** the
ones a person pointing at a new device wants: the device's name, location and
uptime (shown in seconds, not the agent's hundredths), each interface's
operational state and error counts, its byte counters (the 64 bit ones where
the agent has them), the load averages, and any extend rows. It says in its
notes how many suggested points are counters, because a counter on a chart
wants a rate.

Anything else the agent has is still readable: set it up by hand as a tag whose
address is the OID. See [the SNMP driver](/iot/protocols/#snmp) for what a tag
becomes, what a missing object does, and why a wrong v2c community looks like a
dead device.

SNMP is read-only here, always. HotLoop does not send SET.

## BACnet/IP

For a building automation controller, a meter, a thermostat: anything on the IP
network that speaks BACnet. The questions are the device's address, the device
instance if you know it (and then HotLoop refuses a different device answering at
that address), and which network card to send from if the machine has two.

The probe asks the device who it is, reads its object list, and reads every
analog, binary and multi-state object it finds (and the integer, large analog,
accumulator and character string values): name, description, units, present
value and status flags. It shows each with what it read right now, and suggests
the first hundred. Units come across as a label and, where they mean one, a
device class, so a `degrees-celsius` input is a `°C` temperature.

It says in its notes how many objects report a fault (they read bad until the
device clears it) and how many are out of service (they read uncertain, because
the value is what was written to them). A multi-state object's description lists
its states, and its sample shows the state as well as the number.

BACnet is read-only here, always. HotLoop does not write a property, and does
not reach a device behind a BACnet router: see
[the BACnet/IP driver](/iot/protocols/#bacnetip) for what is and isn't covered.

## The flow

Three calls, in order, and the first two save nothing.

1. **Ask.** `GET /api/integrations` lists every integration and its questions.
   Each question has a kind (`text`, `number`, `bool`, `choice` or `secret`), a
   default, whether it is required, and, when it only matters after another
   answer, `showWhen`. A screen is drawn from that and nothing else, which is
   why a new integration needs no new screen.
2. **Look.** `POST /api/integrations/{id}/probe` takes the answers, checks
   them, connects to the real device with the integration's own driver, and
   reports what it is and what it has: a suggested name, what it says about
   itself, notes worth reading, and every point it found as a tag-shaped
   record with a `sample` of what it read, so you can compare it with the
   number on the machine's own display.
3. **Keep.** `POST /api/integrations/{id}/setup` takes the same answers and the
   names of the points to keep (none named keeps the ones marked
   `suggested`), creates the device and its tags and reloads the runtime. The
   device is enabled and polling.

Setup looks at the device again instead of trusting the probe. A client's idea
of what it found a minute ago is a claim, and the points are checked against the
device as it is when the device is made. A name that isn't on it is a `400`, not
a point skipped, because somebody asked for it by name.

A setup that fails part way (the device saved, the tags didn't) removes the
device it just made. A device that already exists is refused with a `400`
rather than overwritten: to add points to a device you have, use its Browse and
Import.

## Answers are checked before anything is tried

The framework checks every answer against its question before an integration
sees it, and reports every problem at once, so a form is fixed once:

* a required question that is blank is "X is required";
* a number must be a whole number inside the question's range, a choice must be
  one of its choices, a bool must be a bool;
* an answer to a question the integration doesn't ask is refused, not ignored,
  because a misspelled `pasword` dropped without a word is a device that fails
  to log in with no hint why;
* a secret may not be the `[redacted]` placeholder the API shows in place of a
  stored one. Sending it back would store the placeholder as the password;
* a question that isn't showing (`showWhen`) is ignored, and isn't required.

Credentials are held the way a device's are: sealed at rest when HotLoop has a
sealing key, and hidden from every API response and every error. A probe never
saves what it was given.

## When the device doesn't answer

`502`, with what went wrong: "could not reach the device: ..." when nothing
connected, "connected, but could not list its points: ..." when it did and
then didn't answer. That is the device's answer to read, not a fault in
HotLoop and not a bad request. A closed port, a wrong community or a firewall
all end up here, and the message is the driver's own.

## Where it sits in the product

Probe and setup reach across the network from the HotLoop box, so both need
`devices.write`, the same as saving a device. Listing needs `devices.read`.
Every product carries them. The routes are in [API.md](/iot/api/#integrations).

## Adding one

An integration is a Go type in `internal/integration` with three methods and a
`Register` call in its `init`:

* `Info()` says what it is: id, name, the driver's protocol, how to ask for
  the address, and the questions;
* `Configure()` turns checked answers into an address and the driver's own
  configuration block, and refuses what a question can't express;
* `Discover()` reaches the real device and reports what is on it.

The framework refuses, at start, an integration that can't be a catalog
entry: a duplicate id, a protocol the model doesn't declare, a question with
no label, a choice with no choices, a default that isn't a valid answer, or a
`showWhen` that names a question that isn't there. A test also holds every
integration to a protocol with a driver compiled in.

An integration doesn't get merged until a test has had it talk to a real
server for that protocol, running in the test lab (`test/services/up.sh`).
Where there is no real server to run, there is no integration, and the
[roadmap](/roadmap/) says which ones are waiting on hardware.
